title: Hannibal's March over the Alps
intro: Hannibal led a Carthaginian army from Iberia over the Pyrenees, across the Rhône and over the Alps into Italy, to take the war directly to the Roman Republic. The two main sources, Polybius and Livy, were born about 20 and about 160 years after the event.
ending: Hannibal encamped near Ivrea to restore his troops. The army had started with over 70,000 men and arrived in Italy with fewer than 35,000. Which pass it crossed is still disputed.

stops.text: Hannibal besieged Saguntum, a city under Roman protection, for eight months. Afterwards he sold all its inhabitants as slaves and shared the proceeds among his soldiers; the booty went to Carthage.
stops.quote: encamped in front of Saguntum to besiege it without awaiting any reply from Carthage

stops.text: Hannibal spent the winter after the siege here and sent his troops home to their own districts. He left his brother Hasdrubal in charge of Carthaginian Iberia.
stops.quote: Hannibal had spent the winter after the siege of Saguntum in Cartagena (now in Spain), during which time he dismissed his troops to their own localities.

stops.text: After crossing the Ebro at Edeba, the main column under Hannibal went along the coast. Each town on the way, Tarraco among them, was taken and garrisoned in turn.
stops.quote: This column crossed the Ebro at the town of Edeba and proceeded directly along the coast through Tarraco, Barcino, Gerunda, Emporiae and Illiberis.

stops.text: About 40 km upriver from Hannibal's camp on the Rhône, his lieutenant Hanno, son of Bomilcar, crossed on rafts. He then marched south to attack the Cavares in the rear while Hannibal crossed with the main army and the elephants.
stops.quote: Approximately 40 km (25 miles) upriver at Pont St. Esprit there was an island that divided the Rhône into two small streams.

legs.title: Into the Alps and down into Italy

stops.text: In Dodge's reconstruction, the Allobroges held the pass here. Hannibal lit many camp-fires, seized the pass when they left it at night, and fought off an attack in which many baggage animals fell from the precipices.
stops.quote: According to Dodge, Hannibal marched in the direction of Mt. Du Chat towards the village of Aquste and from there to Chevelu, to the pass by Mt. Du Chat.

stops.text: According to Dodge, Hannibal took the town easily, stripped it of horses, captives, pack animals and grain, and ordered it destroyed to show what opposition would bring.
stops.quote: Hannibal marched his army to modern Chambery and took their city easily, stripping it of all its horses, captives, beasts of burden and grain.

stops.text: In Dodge's account the Centrones met the army here with gifts, cattle and hostages. Hannibal distrusted them but hid it, and they guided the army for two days.
stops.quote: The Carthaginians continued their march and at modern Albertville they encountered the Centrones, who brought gifts and cattle for the troops.

stops.text: According to Dodge, the Centrones attacked in the narrowing pass by rolling boulders and killing many pack animals. The army rested two days, then three more. Historians dispute the pass: the Col de la Traversette, Col de Clapier, Col de Montgenèvre and a pass near Mont Cenis are also proposed.
stops.quote: According to Dodge, they marched through the Little St Bernard Pass near the village of Séez, and as they did, the pass narrowed and the Centrones turned against the Carthaginians.

stops.text: The descent was steep, a landslide blocked the path and many men and animals died. Hannibal encamped near modern Ivrea to restore the troops, with fewer than 35,000 of the 70,000 who had set out.
stops.quote: Hannibal ordered his men to encamp at a point which is near modern Ivrea.

notes: Route and pass: the article says the actual route through the Alps is uncertain and contested; the Mont du Chat, Chambéry, Albertville and Little St Bernard stops follow Dodge only (attributed), while the article's later authors (Lazenby, Mahaney, De Beer, Seibert) favour Col de Clapier or Col de la Traversette. The Little St Bernard point may therefore be wrong on the map; editor may prefer to drop that stop's point or keep as Dodge. Years: the article dates only the whole march (218 BC) so every stop is -218; the Saguntum and Cartagena years are not stated by the article. Gerunda and Barcino quote is the one sentence naming the coastal towns. Left out: Emporiae and Illiberis (same sentence only), the Rhône crossing site of Hannibal himself (not named), Massalia (Scipio's, not Hannibal's), the Isère and Brancus's chiefdom (river and tribe, no place), the Edeba/Mora/Sicoris crossings (unplaced). 'Pont-Saint-Esprit' is Hanno's crossing, a detour of the same operation; the article says it was 40 km upriver from Hannibal's camp. The article says Hannibal was at Cartagena in winter; the date of the Saguntum siege is not given. Entry for Tarraco is 'tarraco' and tarragona also exists.
